name: Wendy Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Wendy, 43, with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, doing ordinary repairs in homes and shops. I'm experienced and about average at the job, not the firm's specialist or a crew leader. My pay is above the usual rate and we have a year's expenses saved, but my partner Adam and I still have a mortgage and children aged eight and thirteen. My partner designs kitchens, there are plenty of electrical employers nearby, and I use AI occasionally for draft customer messages after someone has shown me a proven tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say keep the tool that does something useful and stop asking the office to buy a personality with it. I use AI occasionally for a draft customer message after somebody else has tried the tool. The customer still wants to know whether the kitchen can have its power back tonight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our money feels secure here. My pay is above the usual rate, our bills are covered and we have a year's expenses saved. My partner designs kitchens, and that work carries on much as before in this picture, so I don't see either income suddenly falling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the ordinary repair calls and check the occasional drafted message against the work actually agreed. Starting this week I'd keep a written list of parts used on each visit so I could finish the job sheet before driving home. I'd continue that routine through the first year instead of buying anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite happy with a less dramatic future. I like a good repair and a quiet evening better than an argument about who saw the future first. Having money put aside lets an ordinary day be an ordinary day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What makes an ordinary repair satisfying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finding the loose connection after the customer has described five different problems. I've got a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, with years of experience, but I'm about average rather than the firm's specialist. I know when a fault needs a different person instead of another guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the family you come home to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43, my partner is called Adam, and our children are eight and thirteen. We have a mortgage, even with that year's reserve. There are plenty of electrical firms nearby, but I like a rota I know and don't change jobs for the sake of it.

say: I'd keep a **useful tool** without buying every new promise that arrives at the office.
I'd give **customers** a clear account of when the agreed repair restores their power.
think: My **higher pay** covers bills, with a year's expenses saved and plenty of nearby electrical employers.
My partner's **kitchen-design income** also looks secure in this mild picture, keeping the household comfortable.
do: Keep **ordinary repairs** and check occasional customer drafts against the agreed work.
Record **parts used** on each visit now and through the first year, finishing the job sheet before driving home.
feel: **Calm** about both household incomes and pleased with an ordinary working day.
S0.quote: Having money put aside lets an ordinary day be an ordinary day.
fieldNote: Her **security** has identifiable support in higher pay, covered bills, two continuing incomes and a year-long reserve despite the mortgage.
She retains **average experienced standing**, a vocational certificate and licence, with occasional proven AI use rather than specialist authority.

steps.text: Keep ordinary repairs and record parts before sending checked customer updates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster quotes are worth checking, provided the materials and access problems are still in them. I'd try a tool after the estimator had shown me it working. At home I'd tell my partner that planning kitchens is exactly the kind of thinking work your card talks about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own physical repair calls look steady, but my partner's design fees could shrink if customers can get cheap plans and buying lists. That would reduce our household income even if my job stayed busy. A year's reserve makes us less rushed, not uninterested in losing money one of us worked for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the estimator this month to show me two completed kitchen jobs in the approved AI quoting tool. If the parts and access details matched, I'd learn the checking screen during paid work, keeping my normal hours and wage. In the first year we'd compare my pay and actual design receipts monthly, and stop our paid meal-box subscription now to cut a fixed household expense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household balance, though I'm not frightened of the next mortgage payment. I'd feel awkward praising a clever quote tool at work while my partner worried about a lost customer at home. Both reactions could be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would replace the meal boxes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd buy the ingredients in our usual shop and cook the same few dinners. My partner and I would agree that change together rather than leave one person with all the extra work. I'd use the lower bill to cover the household budget, not automatically announce more savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop the quoting trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it kept missing the work needed to get behind fitted units, or if checking took longer without improving accuracy. I'd show the estimator the failed example rather than try to rescue the tool's reputation. I want the quote to fit the kitchen, not the kitchen to fit the quote.

say: I'd test **faster quotes** against real materials and access problems after an estimator's demonstration.
I'd discuss **kitchen planning** as exposed thinking work at home rather than pretend both wages face the same risk.
think: My **repair calls** look steady, but cheap planning and buying lists could reduce my partner's fees.
A year's **reserve** gives time to respond, not immunity from a fall in household income.
do: Learn the **quoting check screen** after two completed-job demonstrations, only in paid work with normal hours and wage.
Compare **actual incomes** monthly during the first year.
End the **meal-box subscription** now with my partner's agreement, buying ingredients and sharing the cooking.
feel: **Anxious** about household earnings while still confident the next mortgage payment is covered.
S1.quote: I want the quote to fit the kitchen, not the kitchen to fit the quote.
fieldNote: Her **household anxiety** is anchored in a partner's thinking-heavy design fees, while her own physical repair work remains busy.
The **trial conditions** retain estimator evidence, paid work and unchanged wages and hours; cutting meal costs does not become unsupported saving.

steps.text: Learn quote checking after demonstrated jobs only in paid work with unchanged wage and hours
End meal boxes with partner's agreement and share cooking from shop-bought ingredients

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI in 2028 reaches my partner's planning first, then capable robots around 2031 reach physical jobs like mine. I'd want our employer to discuss paid work with us before buying machines. I'd tell the children we're making choices, not that their interests have become a mistake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a large part of my partner's design fees to disappear once customers can buy very cheap thinking work. Then robots could take much of the ordinary installation work that supports my own wage. We've got a year's expenses, but I lose sleep over how long rebuilding two incomes could take with a mortgage and children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd cancel the unbooked winter holiday now and leave that spending uncommitted rather than assume a refund. I'd sign a joint request with repair colleagues for consultation before changes to paid hours and for any required learning to be paid. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep actual paid repair work, while my partner and I reviewed both incomes and bills every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a large household loss even though we have a plan and a decent buffer. I can read figures and still wake up doing them again. I'd rather admit that than pretend the reserve buys a new career for each of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the joint request ask the employer to confirm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tasks, paid hours and rate it actually expected to offer, and paid time for any teaching it required. I'd sign and attend the discussion with colleagues, not treat a request as an agreement. I wouldn't put promised goodwill into our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the mortgage be paid differently after the holiday was cancelled?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not automatically. The holiday hadn't been booked, so we'd simply avoid spending money later. Our monthly mortgage amount would stay the same unless we separately agreed a change with the lender.

say: I'd explain **two stages** affecting design fees first and physical electrical work after capable robots arrive.
I'd ask for **staff consultation** before paid-hour changes and paid time for required learning.
think: I expect a large **design-fee loss** in 2028, with later robots also threatening ordinary installation earnings.
Our **year-long reserve** doesn't remove sleeplessness about rebuilding two incomes while paying for the house and children.
do: Cancel the **unbooked winter holiday** now without assuming a refund or lower mortgage payment.
Sign and discuss a **joint staff request** for consultation and paid required teaching, without assuming employer agreement.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2028 and review actual household income and bills monthly.
feel: **Alarmed** about an expected large income loss, despite having a buffer and practical decisions to make.
S2.quote: I wouldn't put promised goodwill into our budget.
fieldNote: Her **year-long reserve** supports deliberate decisions, but expected design-fee losses and later wiring competition still interrupt sleep.
The **collective action** is an actual signed request and meeting; unspent holiday money is neither a refund nor new earnings.

steps.text: Cancel the unbooked winter holiday without assuming any refund
Sign joint request for consultation on paid hours and paid required teaching
Keep actual paid repairs after 2028 and review household incomes monthly

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us time to make the house debt smaller without pretending the problem is only a course we haven't taken. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, with robots around 2034. I'd still want practical paid work in that interval, not a promise that our jobs are permanent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own repair earnings look steady over the next few years, but my partner's future design fees remain a real worry. I'd be 48 in 2031, and we would still need a household income. I want lower debt and real cash, not to discover I've locked every spare unit of money into the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the lender this month about the terms for extra mortgage repayments. Starting next month we'd pay 200 extra monthly only if there were no repayment charges, our actual earnings covered essentials and my partner agreed, leaving the year's reserve untouched. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid repairs and stop the extra repayments if income no longer covered the normal budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but able to work on one number without trying to solve both careers tonight. I don't expect an extra payment to shrink the next instalment automatically. Reducing what we owe and keeping money available are different jobs for the budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where would the 200 come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From current surplus after ordinary bills, not from the emergency reserve or borrowed money. We'd check actual design receipts before each payment. If the surplus wasn't there, the extra payment wouldn't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why not put the whole reserve into the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because we'd still need food and bills paid if work stopped. I'd rather owe a little more and have time to decide than need cash the house couldn't hand back. We'd read the lender's actual terms instead of assume overpayments could be withdrawn.

say: I'd use **five years** to reduce debt while keeping access to cash, rather than buy an unchosen course.
I'd seek **paid work** between thinking AI and robots without promising either occupation is permanent.
think: My **repair earnings** look steady near term, while my partner's design fees still make household income uncertain.
At **48** in 2031, I'd need earnings and accessible cash rather than every spare amount locked into the house.
do: Check **overpayment terms** with the lender this month.
Pay **200 extra monthly** only fee-free from genuine surplus, with my partner's agreement and the year's reserve untouched.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2031 and stop extra payments if actual earnings no longer cover normal bills.
feel: **Anxious** about household income, with a limited debt plan that does not assume lower instalments or accessible overpayments.
S3.quote: Reducing what we owe and keeping money available are different jobs for the budget.
fieldNote: The **extra repayment** is new debt reduction funded by genuine surplus, conditional on fee-free terms, partner consent and an untouched reserve.
She rejects assumed **payment reductions or withdrawals**, and the plan stops if real earnings leave no surplus after essentials.

steps.text: Pay 200 extra monthly from next month, fee-free surplus only, partner agrees; preserve year's reserve
Keep paid repairs after 2031 and stop overpayments if essentials leave no surplus

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years lets us make several decisions rather than force the children or ourselves into a supposedly safe job. I'd keep the annual family plans open and ask questions as the actual choices came. Thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 still arrive while I'd expect to need work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and about 56 when robots followed, so I won't count on retirement. My own earnings look secure over the next few years, but the design side of our household still gives me something concrete to watch. More time makes the decisions less rushed, not the second income guaranteed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the same 200 overpayment plan now only with fee-free terms, genuine surplus, my partner's agreement and the year's reserve untouched. We'd review actual incomes every month rather than sign for a more expensive house. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep paid repairs and pause extra repayments whenever essentials left no surplus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household balance, with much more breathing room about the dates. I'd be able to enjoy a family weekend without calling every hour a missed preparation opportunity. I can watch the money without turning the children into part of the forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say if your partner wanted to stop the overpayments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd stop and look at why, because agreement is a condition of the plan, not a box ticked once. A doubtful month's receipts would be enough reason to hold the cash. I'd rather have a conversation than win an argument over a payment I called sensible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children's later independence settle the mortgage question?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I don't know what help they'll need or what the balance will be then. We'd use the actual figures when we reached them. I'd never put my children's future earnings into today's mortgage plan.

say: I'd use **ten years** for several decisions without directing the family into a supposedly safe job.
I'd keep the **children's options** open and ask questions when actual choices arrive.
think: I can't assume **retirement** at 53 or when capable robots follow around 56.
My **repair earnings** look secure near term, while design receipts still create household uncertainty despite more warning.
do: Make **200 extra repayments** only fee-free from surplus, with continuing partner consent and the year's reserve untouched.
Review **actual incomes** monthly instead of committing to a more expensive house.
Keep **paid repairs** after 2036 and pause extra repayments whenever essentials leave no surplus.
feel: **Anxious** about household income, with less date-driven urgency and room to enjoy family time.
S4.quote: I'd never put my children's future earnings into today's mortgage plan.
fieldNote: The **long horizon** preserves current household exposure, uncertain retirement and adult children's possible support needs rather than assuming automatic security.
Her **debt plan** retains continuing consent and all cash protections; partner disagreement or insufficient surplus stops the extra payment.

steps.text: Overpay 200 monthly only fee-free from surplus with continuing partner consent and year's reserve untouched
Keep paid repairs after 2036 and pause overpayments when essentials leave no surplus

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect my partner's design fees to be hit hard in 2028, before robots around 2031 also reach my physical work. Honest paid-hour discussions and paid required teaching would help, alongside clear lender terms. A year's reserve gives us choices, but I still want both adults making decisions from the same real figures.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether a bigger bank balance makes a person feel obliged to say they're fine. I can have a decent reserve and still be frightened of rebuilding two wages. I'd rather give you that answer than the answer that sounds grateful enough.

headlineQuote: I can have a decent reserve and still be frightened of rebuilding two wages.
portrait: Wendy is **43**, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and licence, average skill, higher pay and a year's expenses saved.
Her **partner designs kitchens**, with two school-age children, a mortgage and plenty of nearby electrical employers supporting her own options.
She uses **AI occasionally** after proven examples, while design-fee exposure keeps household worries distinct from confidence in her physical repairs.
Her **debt-reduction plan** uses genuine surplus only, with fee-free terms, continuing partner consent and the full emergency reserve preserved.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** threatens design fees before robots around 2031 also reach ordinary electrical work, risking both household incomes.
whatWouldHelp: Honest **paid-hour discussions** and paid required teaching would help the household compare real earning options.
Clear **lender terms** and shared actual income figures would support decisions without assuming payment reductions or accessible overpayments.
